from: Harrison

On the afternoon and evening of April 19, 1863, a division of Federals under Brig. Gen. John Davidson, a division of Confederates under Brig. Gen. Wade Hampton, and a division or more of Confederates under Maj. Gen. J.E.B. Stuart spent the day encountering each other around the area of closest approach between Falmouth, Virginia, and Fredericksburg.

This sector of the Rappahannock River saw some of the earliest clashes of the war, in spring 1862. The town of Falmouth, foothold of the vast Federal Investment in 1862-1863, heaved with military energy and geared itself for another possible forward movement of the Army of the Potomac. In Fredericksburg, Confederate spirits remained low following the humiliating Mud March of late January.

Maj. Gen. J.E.B. Stuart.

Yet on that sunny Monday in April, the three forces combined could muster just a few thousand men. The sobering casualty lists of recent months would have accounted for a sizable portion of those not present. (The absence of other forces from around Fredericksburg brought the day’s effective total to about 9,000 Federals—spearheaded by the 8^{th} Illinois Cavalry and the 8^{th} Pennsylvania Cavalry, along with the 8^{th} New York Cavalry of Davidson’s command, and a number of Federal and civilian eyewitnesses—and perhaps 4,200 Confederates from Hampton’s and Stuart’s forces.)

Much of the area’s wartime population consisted of African Americans who had escaped from slavery in the months before the April 1863 engagement or in its aftermath, and Union soldiers and civilians who remained after the end of formal hostilities in April 1865. The white citizens of the region—notably those sympathetic to the Confederacy and able to avoid displacement—returned from wartime exile to discover that the once-unquestioned hierarchy of race and class had been turned upside down.

Brig. Gen. John Davidson.

They found, too, that April 19, 1863, had left behind physical reminders of the day’s contest between mounted forces, saber against saber. Some of those remnants can still be found today. One of them in particular has likely been kicked around for more than 150 years, resting forgotten about in a basement or workshop.

Twentieth-century discoveries, twentieth-century interpretations

In the early 1960’s, during an era of “centennial-fever” in local historic preservation but limited regulatory and public scrutiny of the effects on the landscape, a relatively accessible portion of the battlefield known as the Massaponax Church or Primmer Road site was bulldozed for commercial use. Local preservationists believed that the open, sandy ground there—owned in April 1863 by Dr. William T. Pattie—had seen the day’s heaviest losses in John Davidson’s charge against the left wing of Wade Hampton’s command under Col. Laurence S. Baker.

Brig. Gen. Wade Hampton.

By 1962, “rescue archaeology” under the direction of National Park Service curator Carl Reidel had recovered a number of mounted-force artifacts, especially buttons and bullets, but also including mixed sets of accoutrements, gear, and equipment. And as revealed decades later, a local collector salvaged at least two cavalry saber blades from Carl Dunaway, a fellow who aided Reidel’s archaeological work.

Carl Dunaway poses for photographer Joe Brown with a flintlock rifle, the site of the Dr. William T. Pattie house, and a somber sky looming behind. Brown’s car is parked in the bottom right corner. Courtesy of the Central Virginia Battlefields Trust.

My 2016 account of that salvage, “Saber Brightness: Glimpses of a Cavalry Clash Along the Rappahannock,” (in The Fletcher Pratt Library, Civil War Studies: Essays, edited by Robert K. Krick with Elizabeth M. E. Risser, New York: Fordham University Press, 2016) constituted my first concentrated effort to research responsibly one or more complex artifacts of Alfred Waud’s 1863 sketchbook.

Despite Waud’s great reputation for documenting Civil War landscape and combat accurately, researchers in recent years have come to realize that the extensive corpus of his early-1863 sketchbook depicting the Fredericksburg theater is a somewhat more complicated body of evidence than originally thought—not invalidated as a source but requiring greater care and skepticism in its use. The varying shades and temperatures of these complications are worthy of a future post.

What follows here, then, consists of the application of a few new details—not drastic re-interpretations requiring a rewrite of my 2016 findings but, I believe, interesting and useful clarifications.

Waud and Loring: an artist’s sketches and a soldier’s letters

I am grateful for the opportunity to share the story and timeline here (and elsewhere) of the late Sally Mauro’s donation of a saber blade that her father, Tom Loring, found and likely kept from the carnage of April 19, 1863. Tom’s family would have been well aware of his army service, first under the command of Wade Hampton and later in the Confederate navy. Yet the Lorings apparently considered the blade’s original owner, and the story behind the saber, to be things of the distant past whose details Tom preferred not to share.

Further evidence exhumed since 2016, however, suggests to me that Tom himself kickstarted research published in 1962, by National Park Service Historian Ralph Happel, about the deadly encounter of Federal cavalryman Philip Eichelberger, Jr. of the 8^{th} Pennsylvania, and a Confederate opponent who perished in the engagement. In a letter to his mother dated April 28, 1863, and published in a Pennsylvania newspaper in July of that year, Private Eichelberger gave the fullest account by far of the fight.

It is a tale of unyielding combat, human drama, and death from saber thrusts. Yet, unlike subsequent prints describing the skirmish, Eichelberger’s own account does not plainly name himself as the killer of the unknown Confederate whom the Pennsylvanians turned over to their counterparts in the 8^{th} Illinois Cavalry for burial.

Thomas A. Loring, 1863-1864. Courtesy of Kenneth Robison.

Eichelberger’s account, along with an 1883 team sketch by Alfred Waud surviving in an 1886 magazine print, an 1863 oil painting by another artist, and Loring’s saber, all point repeatedly to Hampton’s South Carolina Legion as the command from which the most likely candidate for the saber’s original owner emerged: Lieutenant George L. Stone.

The anomaly of a curved saber blade

The weapon that Tom Loring held in the doorway of “The Sentry Box,” William H. Newman’s shop on Fredericksburg’s Princess Anne Street, was itself an anomaly.  Unlike the sabers of the majority of their opponents on April 19, 1863, the Confederate cavalrymen of Hampton’s South Carolina Legion carried curved sabers, rather than straight ones.

Detail from a post-war team drawing by Alfred Waud, based on his own 1863 sketch of the Rappahannock encounter. This image shows the engagement along Primmer Road (now Virginia Route 633/Dahlgren Road) of the 8th Pennsylvania Cavalry’s Co. L (foreground) and the 8th Illinois Cavalry’s Co. D (partly visible on far right). The “T” path in upper right corner is along the now largely hidden route of Primmer Road across the tracks. Five buildings from left to center constitute a part of the Pattie plantation. Note the severed limb of a tree, lower left, along with two, sapling-size stumps. Author’s collection.

Alfred Waud’s 1883 team sketch depicting the incident. A curved saber is visible in the right hand of the leftmost Federal trooper, at about 7:00 on the saber’s “face.” The leftmost trooper in the background, behind and just to the left of the fallen Confederate trooper and horse, is the 8th Pennsylvania Cavalry’s Lt. John S. Sener; beside him is Captain James H. Breathed of the 8th Pennsylvania’s Co. L. Author’s collection.

Engraving in The Soldier of Liberty, courtesy of the author’s collection.

Artist’s Ralph R. Reeder’s 1966 rendition of Philip Eichelberger, Jr. and Lt. George L. Stone in a scene from the day’s combat. Note Stone’s curved saber. Author’s collection.

From the hour of the engagement onward, the “strange” factor of the South Carolinian sabers made a strong impression not only on the Federals who encountered them in April 1863 but also on the landscape, where those blades continued to make themselves known beneath the surface.

Carl Dunaway’s efforts to recover more souvenirs of the 1863 charge in the 1940’s and ‘50’s produced two highly prized trophies: a pair of curved saber blades. Sometime following closure of the second of the two trench-line scars on the Pattie tract, sometime between 1961 and 1963, he passed both blades along to an area collector named Joey Fulwiler.

    Center, one of Carl Dunaway’s two curved saber blades. Curved saber blade from the South Carolina Legion Cavalry of Wade Hampton. Dunaway found the blade during relic-hunting at the Pattie Tract along Primmer Rd. (VA Rt. 633) near Falmouth, Virginia, where Confederate and Federal cavalry clashed on April 19, 1863. It is the same blade Mr. Dunaway gave to Joey Fulwiler, who in turn gave it to Steve Thomas (private collection). Those to whom Dunaway gave the saber blade referred to it as part of a South Carolina state sword, perhaps due to similar swords found during relic hunting at Brandy Station, Virginia, or possibly in reference to a body of state-issued weapons. I wonder if the Federals at Chancellorsville who dispatched Confederates with the weapons thought they were using ancient relics, rather than a style popular three centuries after Renaissance Europe. As Mr. Thomas has noted, Alfed Waud’s 1883 team sketch of the day’s fight indicates that a curved saber had been retrieved from the field (upper center). Image source: Battle of Fredericksburg by Bruce Catton (Garden City, NY: Doubleday & Company, Inc., 1950-60), 116. The image of the saber courtesy of Clarence A. (“Clar”) Geier. Used with permission.

A long-awaited identification

I wonder what thoughts flitted through the young Confederate naval recruit’s mind as he stood victorious over the prone Confederate, whose blood-coated saber he perhaps extricated from the sandy bottomland to keep as his prize. Many decades later, Tom’s daughter, Sally, and her own daughter Jennifer (Logwood) proved eager and able to explore the possibility that Tom had retrieved that very saber and kept it within the family collection presented to the National Park after her death.

Some of the inscribed graffiti on Loring’s saber had faded over the long span of time separating it from April 19, 1863. Some of it remained plainly visible, however, and a few helpful comparisons could be made:

Author’s collection.

Author’s collection.

Author’s collection.

Lastly, forensic anthropology can identify individuals from bones and teeth, although post-battle dental records of Civil War soldiers are hard to come by. Yet it is far from impossible that an intimate familiarity with Loring’s saber blade, combined with a chance to examine any surviving remains, might identify positively, or at least suggest strongly the original owner.

Some historians, including myself, would offer the strong possibility that a surviving signature different from Hampton’s South Carolina Legion might indicate a specific individual, and that this evidence might support a successful search among the known burial places and family papers of the Confederate dead for a particular individual who was present on the field on April 19, 1863.

Forensic examination of the saber took place in December 2019-February 2020. Although a final report has not yet appeared, Linda Gibbons Sheffield and Beverly Penovich shared some of their findings in a presentation of late 2019:

- Eleven different unsharpened and sharpened cutting edges on the saber’s tip, suggesting that this particular blade had been used for more than a decoration or showpiece…
- Extreme signs of gouging from the edge of a burial spade on the saber’s upper and more extensively accessible (outermost) curve, near the flat. Such signs would support any nearby, known accounts of burial details encamped on the field in the days after the engagement…
- And, most tantalizingly, microscopic evidence of the presence of horse blood on Loring’s saber. The evidence is too limited, however, to determine whether or not a human victim’s blood might also have been found (and preserved) on the blade.

More to come, I hope, on Tom Loring’s saber—a retired athlete just beginning its new career as a forensic tour-de-force.

Noel G. Harrison
